deepSections.title: Foehn mechanics and surface traces
paragraphs: When mid-latitude westerlies impinge on the Black Hills, stable flow can descend lee slopes as a warm, dry downslope wind. In narrow valleys, the replacement of cold pool air happens quickly enough to produce step changes in temperature readings that are visible on minute-resolution archives.
These are not merely ‘nice warm days’ — they are adiabatic warming events with real implications for snowmelt, road ice, and wildfire risk when relative humidity crashes.

deepSections.title: Ecotone fire and water
paragraphs: Spearfish sits where ponderosa pine meets grassland — a boundary that moves with fire frequency and winter moisture. Climate warming pushes some processes toward more rain-dominated winter precipitation, which changes both fire season length and plant recruitment.
Management here is applied climatology: fuel treatments, water rights, and recreation economies all depend on how snow and wind regimes shift together.

deepSections.title: Ventilation, pooling, and humidity
paragraphs: Cold-air pools in humid eastern climates differ from intermountain-west basins: longwave cooling still drives surface stratification, but soil moisture and cloud feedbacks can either reinforce or erode the pool depending on synoptic wind.

Burkes Garden’s nearly closed geometry limits horizontal ventilation until pressure gradients strengthen — a situation where a few meters of elevation change can mean the difference between liquid dew and rime on crops.

deepSections.title: Floor vs rim farming
paragraphs: Hay and pasture dominate the floor because risk management is simpler at scale than tree fruit with late-spring radiation freezes. Rim sites catch earlier spring sun and avoid the deepest pools — classic thermal-belt logic transposed onto a sinkhole landform.
Climate change does not remove the pool; it changes the frequency of destructive freeze events relative to phenological advance — the central problem of eastern orchardists everywhere.

deepSections.title: The Balcones Escarpment and the city's heat
paragraphs: Austin sits on the Balcones Escarpment, the line where the limestone Hill Country drops to the coastal prairie. Humid air from the Gulf is lifted along that line, and that lift is one reason storms here can stall and drop extreme rain. The city itself holds heat. Pavement and buildings keep summer nights warmer in the centre than in the hills to the west.

The two sides of town differ. West of the escarpment the ground is thin soil over limestone, with oak and juniper, cooler nights and a higher wildfire risk. East of Interstate 35 it is deep black clay prairie, flatter and more humid. The Colorado River and its lakes run between them, and the creeks that feed the river are where flash floods happen.

deepSections.title: Water supply, flood and heat
paragraphs: Austin's water comes from the Highland Lakes on the Colorado River, managed by the Lower Colorado River Authority. In the drought of 2011, the driest year on record in Texas, the lakes fell far below normal and stayed low for years. How much more growth the lakes and the Edwards Aquifer can support is the region's long-term question.

The hazards come in more than one form. Floods on Onion Creek in 2013 and 2015 destroyed hundreds of homes, the freeze of February 2021 cut power and water for days, and the summer of 2023 brought weeks of afternoons above 38°C. When looking at a property, check its floodplain status, the wildfire risk on the western edge, and what it costs to cool.

deepSections.title: Alaska scale, city services
paragraphs: Anchorage holds about 290,000 people, roughly two in five Alaskans. Providence Alaska Medical Center is the largest hospital in the state, Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport is its main air gateway, and much of the state's freight arrives through the Port of Alaska.

It is still a long way from anywhere else. Nearly everything is shipped or flown in, and prices show it. On the shortest day the sun is up for about five and a half hours. Snow totals about 200 cm in a winter and lies from late autumn into April.

deepSections.title: Milder than the interior, with earthquakes and avalanches
paragraphs: Cook Inlet and the Chugach Mountains keep Anchorage milder than interior Alaska. January nights average about −12°C here and about −25°C in Fairbanks. Summer afternoons average 19 to 20°C, with daylight late into the evening.

The ground is the main hazard. The 1964 earthquake, magnitude 9.2, destroyed parts of downtown and the Turnagain neighborhood where the clay beneath them gave way, and a magnitude 7.1 earthquake in 2018 damaged roads and buildings. Hillside neighborhoods face wildfire and strong winds off the Chugach, and avalanches close the Seward Highway in some winters.
